doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Children dancing to Thelonious Monk
summary: Palmer plays Monk for young classes and the children dance; Rowe recalls hearing Monk on the radio.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: I think you’re right. And among the things I’ve done, one of the toughest was learning how to deal with like kindergarten and first grade classes. You know if you can figure that out, that makes a lot of other things just seem easy.

Yup. Um hum. Yup. I had a few of those classes, and every semester when I was teaching in Boston I always bring in music. You know we learn how to plan everything but I’ll say okay we’ve got to listen to some music. So I’d sit them all down, I’d put on a recording of Monk — Thelonious Monk — and I’d tell the kids, “Okay, when this music comes on do whatever you want to do, just don’t hurt anybody.” And nine times out of ten they all danced to Monk. And so I was like okay, this is what the music does for people when they don’t have any inhibitions. You know? They always would dance. It’s like okay, that’s what it is.

That’s a heck of a coincidence because last night on the way home they were playing Thelonious Monk on the Sirius jazz station and it was so — he was really into hitting these chords where no one else would do it and, you know, Charlie Rouse was, I mean the whole thing was very physical. And so I can almost picture that class you are talking about.
